---
title: "Hands-on: Measuring How Small the World Is"
---

You now know what average path length and clustering mean. Here you measure
them, on networks whose answers you can check by hand and on networks large
enough that you cannot.

::: {.callout-note title="Where the code lives"}
This course keeps its lecture note free of runnable code. Everything you
execute lives in a marimo notebook, so it stays interactive and reactive
instead of being a wall of output frozen into a web page.

**[Run this notebook]({{< var molab.m02 >}})** — it runs in your browser, with

while Python itself is downloaded.

Prefer to work locally? The notebook is in the repository at
[`notebooks/m02-small-world/coding.py`](https://github.com/skojaku/adv-net-sci/blob/main/notebooks/m02-small-world/coding.py).
Run it with `marimo edit notebooks/m02-small-world/coding.py`.
:::

## What you will build

1. Build a graph in [igraph](https://python.igraph.org/en/stable/) from an edge list, then compute shortest paths and pull out connected components. The library is new; the concepts are the ones from Module 1 and from the previous page.
2. Compute local, average-local and global clustering, and reconcile the three by hand on the small graph before trusting the function.
3. Generate ring lattices, Erdős-Rényi random graphs and Watts-Strogatz networks, and compare their clustering and path length side by side.

## What to watch for

- Average local clustering and global clustering will disagree. Work out which nodes cause the gap before reading on — the six-node example on the [concepts page](01-concepts.qmd) gives 0.70 and 0.43 for the same network.
- The ring lattice and the random graph sit at opposite extremes. Note how far each is from the network you would actually want to live in.
